chunks: Al-Hasan ibn Mahbub from Ibn Sinan, he said: Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said:
Amir al-Mu'minin (peace be upon him) ruled regarding one who manumits a slave by contract (kitabah) that he may stipulate his walayah (right of inheritance/guardianship) if he contracts with him.

And he said: 'When the slave is freed as a sa'ibah (freeing himself by paying a sum), there is no walayah upon him for anyone if he dislikes that, and he does not inherit anyone except whom he loves to inherit him.'

So if he loves that his wali al-ni'mah (benefactor) or another should inherit him, let him witness two men regarding the guarantee of what befalls him for every fault he incurs or incident that occurs.
So if the master does not do that and does not transfer [the right] to anyone, then his inheritance is returned to the Imam of the Muslims.

key_terms.إمام المسلمين: The Imam of the Muslims, who inherits if no one else claims
key_terms.سائبة: A slave who frees himself by paying a lump sum
key_terms.كاتب: A slave who has contracted to pay a sum for his freedom
key_terms.ولي النعمة: The benefactor or master who granted freedom

ai.seo_question: What are the rules of inheritance and walayah between a master and a slave in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (AS) elaborates on Imam Ali’s (AS) juridical ruling regarding the *kitabah* contract, distinguishing between the master's stipulated right of inheritance and the freed slave's autonomy as a *sa'ibah* (one freed without compensation). The narration highlights the procedural requirement of two witnesses to guarantee the master's liability for the slave's debts, ensuring that if no heir is chosen, the estate reverts to the Imam, reflecting the Shia emphasis on the Imam's role as the ultimate guardian of property and justice.
